name: Zoe Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at six on the injection moulding floor at Calder Plastics, making housings for medical devices. I set up the tool on Press 4, check the first parts against the gauge, then watch the cycle and tweak the temperature as the day warms up. I'm the shop steward too, so half my lunch break is other people's problems. My knees are what wear me out, not the work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Getting a tricky mould to run clean. Nobody taught me that from a book; it's feel, listening to the press and reading the shine on a part. Young Danny on my shift is learning it from me, and that's the best part of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same old story, a lot of noise from salesmen. At work we've had software 'transformations' before and they mostly gave us more forms. I'd tell people to keep their heads down and keep making good parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's fine for me. I'm 58, I have about four years to go, and the savings are solid. My worry is only that the owners use the word AI to squeeze the new starters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do nothing different. Same shift, same press, I'd keep training Danny, and I'd keep paying into the union fund like always. I'd use the time to book the trip to see my sister in Cardiff I keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored by the whole subject, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the union. How would that come into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union would watch for the owners cutting jobs and blaming a computer for it. We did that in 2012 with the new scheduling system. If they try it, I'll be the one at the meeting asking for the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ravi says I should stop volunteering for everything and just enjoy the last years. He's probably right, but I've never been able to walk past a notice board.

say: It's mostly **hype** from salesmen; we've heard it before.
I tell people to keep making good parts and keep their heads down.
think: I'm safe: about **four years** left and good savings.
I only worry the owners use AI as an excuse to squeeze new starters.
do: Keep paying into the union fund and watch for cuts blamed on software.
Book the long-promised **trip** to Cardiff to see my sister.
feel: Mostly **calm**, and a little bored by the whole subject.
S0.quote: We've had software transformations before and they mostly gave us more forms.
fieldNote: Dismissive of tech talk, but her real **concern** is the owners misusing it against newer workers.
**Steward** identity runs through everything, even a calm scenario.
Savings and age make her genuinely secure here.

steps.text: Keep running Press 4 and training Danny on mould set-ups
Ask the owners for staffing numbers at the next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will feel it first, not the floor. Planning, ordering resin, the quality paperwork. We still have a bloke in the back office, Gareth, who does nothing but order and schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the machines on my floor stay because they need a person to handle the odd mould and the odd resin batch. But I'd be lying if I said I didn't count how many operators the owners think they need per shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written agreement that nobody is let go because of software without six months' notice and retraining paid. I wouldn't touch the new tools myself; if they want my set-ups in a program they can ask me to my face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not my job, it's the lad's job and Gareth's. It sits on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your plant would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth first, then the quality inspectors who sign off the first-off checks. The checking is exactly the kind of thing the salesmen say software does. I'd want them offered a move to the floor, not a pension and a handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the new tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't use AI and I don't plan to. If the line needs it, someone on the line who wants it can do it, and I'll check their work.

say: The **office** will feel it first, not the floor.
We need a written agreement before anyone loses a job to software.
think: My floor stays for now, but I count the **operators** the owners want per shift.
Gareth and the quality inspectors are the people I'd worry about.
do: Push the union for six months' **notice** and paid retraining.
Offer the inspectors a move onto the floor.
Refuse to use the new tools myself.
feel: **Uneasy**, because it hits colleagues more than me.
S1.quote: If they want my set-ups in a program they can ask me to my face.
fieldNote: **Resistant** to tools but constructive about protecting others.
Thinks in terms of named colleagues, not abstract jobs.
Her own job feels safe; the **unease** is about the shop.

steps.text: Press the union for six months' notice and paid retraining
Back the party that promises a retraining levy on factories
Keep running Press 4 and training Danny

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need laws and we need them now. Two years isn't enough for anyone to retrain, never mind a whole town of operators. I'd be at the council meeting saying the factories shouldn't be allowed to cut people before there's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots around 2031 are the real thing for me. The thinking AI takes the office in 2028, but a robot that can change a mould and clear a jam is what ends my job, and I'd be 63. That's right on the edge of when I'd want to stop anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into the union: demand a transition fund, a four-day week with no pay cut, and early retirement at full pension for people over 55. I'd also stop spending on anything big, no new kitchen, and keep a year of wages in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm okay myself, but the plant has 300 people and half of them have mortgages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, because he's 24 and I'd be walking out the door while he's still paying off a van. I'd tell him to learn anything with a licence, like electrics, which the robots will take later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the law change in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years doesn't give time to change the law. Governments take that long to agree what a form should say. We'd get the robots before we got the rules.

say: We need **laws** now; two years isn't enough for a whole town to retrain.
Demand a transition fund and early retirement for the over 55s.
think: The **robots** around 2031 are what end my job, when I'd be 63.
Danny is 24 and would be left with the bills.
do: Go to the **council** meeting and push for a plan before cuts.
Hold a full year of wages in the bank and skip the new kitchen.
Tell Danny to learn a licensed trade like electrics.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly for the 300 people at the plant and Danny.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough for anyone to retrain, never mind a whole town of operators.
fieldNote: Makes the key **distinction** between thinking AI in 2028 and robots in 2031 on her own.
Anxiety is about the community, not her own pot of savings.
Policy-minded: unions and law first, not personal tools.

steps.text: Demand a transition fund and early pensions at the next union meeting
Speak at the council meeting about a plan before factory cuts
Ask HR for the early retirement terms at 60
Keep a full year of wages in the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I'd say is workable if people start now. I'd tell my union branch to put it on every agenda and press the owners for a training scheme that starts this year, not the year it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still be 63 when robots arrive in 2034, and that's close enough to retirement that I'd probably be gone by then. The anxiety is that the plant sells or restructures in between and my pension isn't protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and ask HR to explain the pension in plain numbers, and keep the savings where they are. I'd get Danny and two others on a technical course at the college, paid by the plant if the union can get it. And I'd write to my MP, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious but with a plan. It's the plan that makes the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want involved in the planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college, the union and the owners all at one table, with the people who run the machines. Not consultants in nice shirts who've never changed a mould.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years give you that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be negotiating in a panic. With five I can get terms written down, and I can sit on a bench with Danny and teach him what I know before I go.

say: Five years is **workable** if the union and the owners start the training now.
Put it on every agenda and demand a scheme this year.
think: I'd be 63 when robots arrive, so I'm probably gone by then.
My fear is a **restructure** before my pension is protected.
do: Ask HR to explain my **pension** in plain numbers.
Get Danny and two others onto a technical college course.
Write to my MP for the first time.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, because a plan makes the difference.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be negotiating in a panic. With five I can get terms written down
fieldNote: **Time** converts panic into negotiation for her.
Her own retirement date is a quiet comfort she keeps mentioning.
Wants the people on the machines at the planning table.

steps.text: Ask HR for the pension figures in plain numbers
Get Danny and two others onto a college technical course
Write to my MP about protecting factory pensions
Table the training scheme at every union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different conversation. I'd say it gives the country time to do this properly, with proper training and fair taxes on the firms that gain. I'd hope the unions are strong enough by then to be at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully I'll be 68 in 2036 and long retired, so it's not my job on the line. My grandchildren's world, and Danny's, bothers me more than anything in the first scenarios.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on working to about 62, put money away for the grandkids' training, and spend my free time recruiting younger workers into the union. I'd also probably help the plant write a proper handover so the knowledge doesn't walk out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about me, uneasy about the world they inherit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think about when you look ten years out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, my niece Leila who is thinking about nursing, and the apprentices. I'd tell them to pick work where people matter to other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope is different in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies that share what they save from robots, with the people who made the company. That's what I'd fight for, even from my armchair.

say: Ten years gives the country time to do it properly, with training and **fair taxes** on firms that gain.
I'd hope the unions are strong enough to be at the table.
think: I'll be long retired, so it's my **grandchildren's** world that bothers me.
Danny's future worries me more than my own.
do: Work until about **62** and then retire.
Write a proper handover so my knowledge stays at the plant.
Recruit younger workers into the union.
feel: **Calm** about me, uneasy about the world the young inherit.
S4.quote: My grandchildren's world, and Danny's, bothers me more than anything in the first scenarios.
fieldNote: The **longest** horizon moves her concern from herself to the young.
Genuinely secure personally, but she carries others' worries.
Hopeful about collective action as the answer.

steps.text: Work until 62 and then take the full pension
Write a handover guide for Press 4 for Danny
Recruit young starters into the union at the plant
Set money aside for the grandchildren's training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. It's the one where nobody has time to do anything and the owners run the show. What would help is a law that says firms must give notice and pay for retraining, and a union at every plant to make them keep to it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against machines. I've worked with them my whole life and I like them. It's who gets the benefit that I care about, and who's asked before it happens.

headlineQuote: I'm not against machines. I've worked with them my whole life and I like them.
portrait: Zoe (**58**, shop steward on a medical-plastics floor) is secure personally, with strong savings and about four years to retirement.
Her worries are collective: colleagues in the office, young starters like Danny, and a **300-person** plant.
She resists AI tools herself and says she never uses them, but she is constructive about protecting others.
She turns to the **union** and the law first, pressing harder for paid notice and retraining as AGI comes closer.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most because nobody has time to plan and the owners decide alone.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** requiring notice and paid retraining, plus a union at every plant to enforce it.
